column1: A ball is launched at 20 m/s at 30° above horizontal. What velocity value do you use for its VERTICAL motion?

column1: A ball is dropped from height h, and at the same instant an identical ball is launched horizontally from the same height. Which lands first?
column2: Neither — they land at the same time, since both have the same initial vertical velocity (0) and the same vertical acceleration (-g).

column1: For a projectile launched and landing at the same height, how does horizontal velocity behave during flight?
column2: It stays constant — gravity acts only vertically (a<sub>x</sub> = 0).

column1: For a projectile launched/landing at the same height, how does time-up compare to time-down?
column2: They're equal — the trajectory is symmetric.

column1: A ball is kicked horizontally off a cliff. What determines its time of flight?
column2: Only the vertical motion (height and g) — horizontal velocity has no effect on fall time.

column1: On level ground, what launch angle maximizes range?
On level ground, name two launch angles that give the SAME range.
column2: Any pair that adds to 90° (e.g., 30° and 60°) — since range ∝ sin(2θ).

column1: A projectile is launched from a height above its landing point. Can you use the symmetric shortcut formulas (time up = time down)?
column2: No — launch and landing heights differ, so you must solve Δy = v<sub>y0</sub>t − ½gt² directly for t.

column1: Why can horizontal and vertical motion be analyzed independently in projectile motion?
column2: Because gravity only acts vertically — there's no horizontal force (ignoring air resistance), so the two directions don't affect each other.
